summary: A study in Current Biology found that Caribbean box jellyfish, which lack a central brain, can learn to avoid low-contrast obstacles, the first evidence of associative learning in jellyfish. In tank tests and experiments on isolated rhopalia, the animals and their eye-bearing nerve bundles changed behavior after bumping into obstacles. Outside researchers were enthusiastic but one urged caution because of the small sample, and others discussed what the finding implies for how learning evolved.
one_line: Caribbean box jellyfish without a central brain learned to avoid obstacles, offering the first evidence of associative learning in jellyfish and hints about how learning evolved.
key_facts: Caribbean box jellyfish (Tripedalia cystophora) have no central brain but learned to spot and avoid obstacles in a new study, the first evidence that jellyfish can do associative learning.
Jan Bielecki of Kiel University in Germany and colleagues published the findings September 22 in Current Biology.
Each Caribbean box jellyfish has four rhopalia, and each rhopalium has six "eyes" and about 1,000 neurons to process what the eyes see.
These jellyfish judge a mangrove root's distance by its contrast against the water: nearby roots look high-contrast in clear water, but in murky water even nearby roots can look low-contrast.
The team put 12 jellyfish into a round water tank surrounded by low-contrast gray and white stripes and filmed them for about seven minutes.
The jellyfish's average distance from the tank wall grew from about 2.5 centimeters (1 inch) in the first couple of minutes to 3.6 centimeters (1.4 inch) in the final few minutes.
Their bump rate dropped from 1.8 bumps per minute to 0.78 per minute.
In other tests, snipped-off rhopalia were shown low-contrast gray bars while a weak electrical pulse mimicked a bump; they began sending the signals emitted when a jellyfish darts away.
This suggests the rhopalia alone can learn, hinting that these nerve centers are behind jellyfish learning.
Björn Brembs of the University of Regensburg urged caution, pointing to the small number of jellyfish tested and saying more tests are needed to convince him.
Gaëlle Botton-Amiot asked how learning works given that jellyfish have four rhopalia, and whether losing one means forgetting what it learned.
Botton-Amiot has studied sea anemones, which may also learn; both they and jellyfish are cnidarians, so the ability may be widespread or inherited from a common ancestor.
Nagayasu Nakanishi said learning could also have arisen independently, and comparing the chemicals and mechanisms of learning in different animals could help decide.
